speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ENEMY ATTACK UPON ESTEVAN POINT TELEGRAPH
speechtext: My colleague the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) has some information to give the house with respect to the attack which was made by the enemy off the coast of Vancouver Island on Saturday last. It was the first attack upon Canadian soil that has been made since confederation. There have been attacks upon our ships off the coasts of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and in the gulf and river St. Lawrence, but Saturday night's attack was the first time in this war that our country has been attacked on land. It only goes to bear out what has been said so often that no one can take too seriously both the immediacy and the extent of the danger with which all parts of the world are confronted, and at this time our own part in particular.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: ENEMY ATTACK UPON ESTEVAN POINT TELEGRAPH
speechtext:
A statement was issued yesterday afternoon to the following effect: The commander in chief, west coast defences, reported that the dominion government telegraph station at Estevan Point, Vancouver island, was shelled by a submarine at 10.35 p.m., Pacific time, on Saturday night. No damage resulted. Regarding this incident, a report has been received from the superintendent of the wireless station to the effect that the shelling continued for about forty minutes and that about thirty or more shells fell. From the rate at which the shells were fired it would appear that there were possibly two enemy craft involved. The information also is that Canadian naval and air units operating in that area were ordered to the vicinity at once.
With regard to this matter of the time of release of the information, inquiries were made of the press bureau and the matter was taken up with the intelligence branches of the services, I should like to indicate for the information of members of the house the
Labour Conditions

considerations which are kept in mind in connection with the time of release of information of this kind.
There are always questions with regard to the time of release of information like this, and I should like the house and the public to know that the inclination of all the defence services is to publish the information just as soon as possible after the event. There is, however, this consideration to be kept in mind: as was pointed out by my colleague the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) some little time ago, the publication of these reports by our own services means that we give the enemy news of the operations of their ships, which save those ships reporting direct and thereby risking the giving away of their position. It is, therefore, necessary to determine in each case what time should elapse between the event itself and the public announcement of it. This determination will have to rest to a large extent with the intelligence branches of the services involved. One of the important factors, of course, would be whether the enemy craft was near enough to land to enable its location to be ascertained by the interception of messages. No hard and fast rule can be laid down, as is apparent, and all I can say is that all the services will do everything consistent with security to publish information at the earliest moment practicable.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OP SERVICE OVERSEAS

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, June 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King for the second reading of Bill No. 80, to amend the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Roy.
Hon. ANGUS L. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services): Mr. Speaker, without any doubt or hesitation or reservation whatsoever, I support Bill No. 80. I believe that the repeal of section 3 of the National Resources Mobilization Act is a wise step in itself. I believe, further, that if the vote on the plebiscite question is to be given any meaning, if the efforts and the speeches of many members of this house and of thousands of other good and loyal Canadians during the plebiscite campaign are to be held as anything more than wasted time and meaningless words, section 3 should be repealed. We must remember that the people of Canada, by a majority of more than 1,300,000 votes, have said that, to use the-very words of the plebiscite question, they wished the government to be free "from any past commitments restricting the method of raising men for military service". The people having said that they wished the government to be free, the government now must take the necessary steps to free itself, and that is what the government is endeavouring to do in this bill.
If this bill is passed and the government is thereby freed, I believe that the government should then accept the responsibility for which it asked, by implication at least, in the plebiscite question, and for which it asked directly in the speech from the throne. The words in the speech from the throne which are now relevant are these, with some of the intervening words omitted in order to give perhaps a clearer sense of the meaning:
The government is of the opinion that . . . the administration, subject only to its responsibilities to parliament, should . . . possess com-

Mobilization Act-Mr. Macdonald (Kingston)
plete freedom to act in accordance with its judgment of the needs of the situation as they may arise.
Those were the words of the speech from the throne; "the administration should possess complete freedom to act". I think that only one interpretation can be placed upon these words: the administration should have freedom, freedom to apply conscription for overseas service whenever the occasion should demand. But we must remember this, that true freedom, real freedom, involves the right of choice. Let me illustrate what I mean by a simple figure, to show the government's position. The highways of our country are free and open to all travellers. A wayfarer plans to journey along a road, and on his map he sees a point where that road branches or forks in two directions. Across one of these branches is an insurmountable barrier, and he says, "When I reach that fork I wish to have freedom to take either branch. Therefore remove the barrier, so that I may have freedom to travel as I think best. I cannot say at this moment which road I shall take. That decision will be made when I reach the junction, and will depend on several factors, some of which are largely beyond my control." Now the people of Canada, by their vote on the plebiscite question, have removed the barrier that lay across the road of government policy. They have removed the barrier of past commitments against conscription for overseas service. It must be taken that they wished the government to have power to follow the road of conscription if the government so wished. That much, at least, is implied in the plebiscite vote. And if the plebiscite result did not mean that the government should be free to take that road, then the plebiscite result meant nothing. It represented a waste of time and effort and money.
Mark you, Mr. Speaker, the plebiscite result may not have meant that the government must take that road. On this point there has been much discussion. It is a point which perhaps can never be settled, unless, indeed, by the taking of another vote on the question of conscription or no conscription.
But surely it must be agreed that those who voted "yes" in answer to the plebiscite question contemplated and accepted the possibility of conscription. An hon. member behind me says "that is not so." Then I ask him: "from what did they relieve the government?" They relieved it from past commitments against conscription. Therefore they must have said to the government, "If you wish at some future time to impose conscription, you shall have that right so far as it is within our power to grant it."

speechtext: That was the very minimum.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OP SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Many of them may have said to themselves, and no doubt did say, "We do not order or direct you to apply conscription." I think many people said to themselves, "We cannot settle these great questions. Let the government settle them. Let the government be free to settle them according to its best judgment. Let it take the road of conscription or the road of no conscription, but let it be free." That is what I think was in the mind of the overwhelming majority of those people who voted "yes".
I must say that some of the statements made in this house and elsewhere on this question in the last few months and weeks are very difficult, for me at least, to understand. One who listened to the debates in this house last week and the week before or who read the reports of these debates might well gain the impression that the majority of hon. members were against conscription in any circumstances whatever. That impression might well, I say, have been gained by reading or listening to those speeches. Some speakers, indeed, have openly stated that that was their view. Others, while stating that they would support conscription if it became absolutely necessary, proceeded to damn conscription with the faintest possible sort of praise. Still others discussed the wisdom of applying conscription now, at this particular moment. They talked as if conscription were likely to be applied to-morrow. I should like to deal with some of these points and with a few others which have arisen from time to time in this connection.
I take, first, the argument as to the efficacy of conscription for overseas service. It has been said that conscription has no value or very little value, that it will not increase in any appreciable degree the number of men available for overseas service, that it has only a very limited, a very small place, in the totality of our war effort. Now, if these arguments are valid; if conscription is no good or of very minor good at any time, we have wasted much valuable time in discussing conscription. The reference in the speech from the throne to the government being free from past commitments was a wholly unnecessary reference. There is not much sense in asking to be free to do something which in the long run will amount to nothing. Similarly, the introduction of the plebiscite bill and the holding of the plebiscite were wholly unnecessary moves. If conscription is of no value and cannot be of any value, then the plebiscite was of no value.
3510	COMMONS
Mobilization Act-Mr. Macdonald (Kingston)
It was worse than valueless. It had a definite minus value, because it cost money, required time, required energy, stirred up feelings, and created bitternesses that had much better never have been born. If conscription is of no value it was foolish to seek release from a pledge against it.
In the second place it is said that conscription will be useless so far as the navy and the air force are concerned, that you cannot force a man to be a sailor or an airman. Now in Great Britain, as I understand the situation there, every man between the ages of eighteen and a half and fifty-one years is subject to conscription. Once conscripted, he is asked which branch of the service he prefers-navy, army or air force-and so far as is possible his wishes are gratified. I should hope that the Royal Navy is not altogether forgotten by those men who are conscripted, nor the Royal Air Force; and I should further hope, and my hope has been justified- by events, that when these men get into the Royal Navy or the Royal Air Force they are able to acquit themselves worthily. There is, of course, complete conscription in enemy countries, and their air forces and their armies and their navies have done, I regret to say, somewhat too well for my liking in many instances. Furthermore, I think my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) will agree that it is an unjust and- unwarranted reflection on the army to suggest that men may not be good enough for the navy and the air force but still good enough for his service.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OP SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
It
is pointed out in the third place that Northern Ireland, South Africa and Australia have not adopted the system of compulsory service overseas. I observe with considerable interest that our sister dominion of New Zealand is not on that roll: she is not there because for nearly two years that dominion has had conscription for overseas service, and I would remind my hon. friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation-what they already know, of course-that New Zealand in those years has had a labour government. It is quite correct to say that Northern Ireland, South Africa and Australia still follow the voluntary system so far as overseas service is concerned. But what about our other allies? What about Great Britain? What about the United States? What about Russia? There is conscription in every one of those countries. What about our enemies- Germany, Italy, and Japan? They all have conscription. In fact, it can be" said truthfully 
that practically every European country when it became engaged in war adopted the compulsory system; and it seems to me that the example of Northern Ireland and of our sister dominions of South Africa and Australia is hardly an infallible guide against such a weight of contrary evidence from those other great countries.
In the fourth place, Mr. Speaker, it is said we should not have conscription for overseas service because it would interfere with our industrial production and our agricultural production. Somewhat similar was the argument advanced by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation at the beginning of the war. His party wished to see a sort of economic war by Canada with no men going overseas, either voluntarily or by conscription. The general argument as to industry and agriculture can be answered in many ways, but I shall refer to only two.
First, even if we were to adopt the principle of overseas service now and put it into practice later, we should not, we must not, strip our factories and our farms of workers. War industries of course must continue; agriculture must be maintained if the war is to go on, and I think it is merely raising a weak sort of bogey to say it would be otherwise.
The second answer is one that was presented on Friday last in this chamber by the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald). It was advanced two years ago in the debate on the National Resources Mobilization Act by my hon. friend the former Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), who said he thought it was a very low sort of patriotism, a very poor sort of patriotism, that said: "We will confine ourselves to the economic side, to agricultural and industrial production, while others do the fighting." My hon. friend from Brantford City says the same thing, and he made this point, that if every nation took that attitude there would be no one to fight. If Russia said: "We are a great agricultural country; we can produce wheat; we also have great industries here, and we can produce implements of war; let the United States and England do the fighting," and if the United States and Britain and the rest took the same attitude, nobody would be left to fight. Tanks are necessary, of course, in this sort of war; planes are necessary; ships are necessary. But tanks in a factory, planes in a hangar, ships on a shipway, gitns in a plant, never yet won a war, and they never will. You must have men to operate these before they become effective.
The real truth is that successful warfare involves the work of both civilians and members of the armed forces. Some men

Mobilization Act-Mr. Macdonald (Kingston)
must work on the farms, some men must work in the factories, and others must fight; and the two sorts of effort must be properly coordinated. What is needed in warfare is *what the Prime Minister has properly described as a balanced effort. You will not have a balanced effort in this country if you devote all the energies of your people to industrial and agricultural production, and certainly you will not have a balanced effort if you put all your men into uniform, whether for service within Canada or outside.
Then it has been argued that if conscription is to be enforced, its actual imposition should come about only by direct action of this parliament. As I understand the argument, it comes to this, that what we say or do now amounts to very little. Here and now in this debate we are merely deciding some sort of philosophic principle, the practical application of which cannot be made until this parliament meets again or until this parliament has had a second discussion and decided that the moment has come to apply conscription. That view has been set forth by the member for Rosetown-Biggar, the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell), and by some of his followers. They argue that it is undemocratic to leave to the government the power to decide by order in council at what moment conscription should be imposed.
It must be remembered-and this has been pointed out before many times in this house, a few days ago by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself-that this government now has the power to conscript persons, their services and1 their property. It has complete power in the matter of conscription except in one respect, and that is that it cannot conscript persons for military service outside Canada and Canada's territorial waters. That is the only restriction upon the powers of this government, and that is the restriction which Bill No. SO seeks to remove.
Members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and some other members of this house profess to find in this bill a principle that is undemocratic. For some reason or other the theory has been spread abroad, or has grown up by itself, that there is some peculiar difficulty or some particular obstacle involved in troops crossing the water or at any rate over any considerable body of, water. There was an old superstition that if you were pursued by a witch the wise and cautious thing to do was to get a running stream between you and the witch. The witch could not cross the water. I hope
that many people read Bums in these times, because he was the prince of the poets of the people. He was one of the greatest of democrats. He has immortalized this superstition in his poem "Tam O'Shanter". It will be recalled by Burns' readers that Tam O'Shanter, after a drinking bout with his old soldier friend in the tavern, was returning home when he was pursued by witches, one of whom outsped the rest. Tam spurred his mare in order to reach the bridge which spanned the river Doon. The witch of course was equally anxious to catch Tam before he reached the bridge, and in one frantic leap she seized the grey mare's tail and carried it off, but the grey mare carried Tam safely across.
There seems to be general agreement here that it is all very well to send troops to Alaska or to any other point in the United States, but when it comes to sending troops across the water, across the Atlantic, you are going into an entirely new field. I would say to my hon. friend of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation that in 1940 they raised no objection to the National Resources Mobilization Act in so far as conscription of men was concerned. I will agree that they said that if you are to conscript men you must first conscript industry and finance.

That is not all my hon. friends say. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation have declared themselves ready to resort to other measures of conscription, certain other types of regi-mention, and these were outlined by the leader of the party not later than a few days ago in this house. He said his group believed in nationalizing all financial institutions. It
3512	COMMONS
Mobilization Act-Mr. Macdonald (Kingston)
believed in compulsory loans, interest free; it believed in government ownership or government control of all essential war industries; it believed in a 100 per cent tax on all profits, and it sought to establish what is called a maximum-minimum income. All these proposals represent very considerable measures of compulsion or regimentation, and it seems to me that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, when it speaks now of the undemocratic spirit which is manifest in this bill, is merely straining at the gnat of compulsory service overseas while it swallows the camel of those other far-reaching measures of compulsion to which I have just referred.
It is said now that we should come back to parliament even after this debate is concluded and submit to parliament the direct question whether we should have conscription at that time.

speechtext: Who has raised that question? We have not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OP SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
1 agree that my hon. friend has not raised it, but it has been said and he knows it has been said both in this house and elsewhere. I regard a second debate on this question as unnecessary. The question has been before the people in one form or another for nearly three years. It has been before the house directly since January 23 last, when the speech from the throne was read. We have had a plebiscite on it, and I must confess that I felt that if the vote on the plebiscite were in the affirmative, there would be very little further debate on the matter. The people would have registered their verdict and parliament would endeavour to give effect to that verdict. That was my view.
We talk a great deal about democracy in these days, and it is well that we should; but I wonder whether democracy is doing itself any service by spending the greater part of five months in the discussion of a question of this sort in times like the present. For my part, on this point of going back to the house a second time I take my stand on the words of the Prime Minister, spoken in this house on June 10. First he quoted from his speech ol February 25 in which he had used these words-Hansard, page 3234:
When we find that we cannot raise the required numbers of men for enlistment overseas by the voluntary method, and it is absolutely necessary to raise more men by other methods, then we will make our decision, present it to parliament and have it discussed on its merits.

After making that quotation from his February speech the Prime Minister went on to say:
Unless the question of conscription for overseas service is to be twice debated, that, as I see it, is the stage we have now reached. The government is making its policy with respect to the raising of men for service overseas fully known. We are presenting that policy to parliament.
That is the stand I take now. There should be no second debate on this question. Those who say that parliament should be consulted again put themselves in rather a curious position, it seems to me. Let us suppose there should be a second debate in this parliament, and that the debate should determine that the time had come when the application of the principle of conscription for overseas service should be made; is it to be expected that even at that stage every detail of the plan would be laid before parliament? Is it to be held that every time a unit is to be sent overseas the matter will be referred to parliament for decision as to whether or not it should go? It seems to me that the proper function of parliament in these as in other cases is to decide general principles, leaving such matters as the time of application of those principles, the numbers of men involved and other details of the kind, to be decided by the governor in council, the decisions of the governor in council, being of course later submitted to parliament, as is required by the National Resources Mobilization Act.
Again there are some who say-not so many now as there were at one time, but still there are some-that this war is an imperialistic war, that it is England's war, a war in which Canadians who are not of British birth or origin can be expected to show only little interest. How can it be truly said that this is an imperialistic war, whether you take the word "imperialism" in its territorial or its financial sense? What evidence is there that the government of the United Kingdom in September, 1939, had any territorial ambitions when it declared war? It did not wish to acquire any territory; indeed it has had a hard enough time during recent months in dealing with some of the territory it already has. No; the United Kingdom government went to war because it was bound by treaty to Poland, just as it was bound by treaty to Belgium in 1914; and the government of Britain made good its bond in 1939 as it had done twenty-five years earlier. Imperialism! Did France want territory, or Belgium, or Holland, or Norway, or any of the other countries that have been overrun by Germany? Did the United States hunger for more land? No; the United States took up the sword because it had been attacked treacherously and in the worst possible faith by the empire of Japan.

Mobilization Act-Mr. Macdonald (Kingston)
On that point as to whether this is an imperialistic war, let me quote three paragraphs from the Atlantic charter to show what is the real policy of Great Britain and the United States:
Their countries-
This is the Prime Minister of Great Britain and the President of the United States speaking.
4.	Their countries seek no aggrandisement, territorial or other.
5.	They desire to bring about the fullest
collaboration between all nations in the economic field with the object of securing, for all, improved labour standards, economic adjustment, and social security.	[DOT]
6.	After the final destruction of the nazi tyranny, they hope to see established a peace which will afford to all nations the means of dwelling in safety within their own boundaries, and which will afford assurance that all the men in all the lands may live out their lives in freedom from fear and want.
That is the Atlantic charter. I follow that with a passage from the agreement entered into by the twenty-six united nations as published at Washington on January 1 of this year. The united nations state that-
. .	. complete victory over their enemies is
essential to defend life, liberty, independence and religious freedom and to preserve human rights and justice in their own lands as well as in other lands, and that they are now engaged in a common struggle against savage and brutal forces seeking to subjugate the world.
Then eveiy one of the twenty-six governments pledged themselves to "employ its full resources, military or economic, against the members of the tripartite pact and its adherents with which such government is at war". Now, under that agreement-and Canada is a signatory to it-we must employ our whole resources, military or economic. We are to supply not merely munitions, not merely food, but men as well, to the common task.
No; this is not an imperialistic war. This is a Canadian war, a war which we entered as a free nation by the free vote of this parliament. It is a Canadian war just as truly as it . is an English or a United States or a Russian war.
If anybody has any doubts whatever as to whether this is a Canadian war, let him remember the news that has come to us within the last twenty-four hours. Our territory has been attacked by a hostile power. The Japanese evidently regard this as a Canadian war. So do the Germans. So do the German submarines that sank ships at the very entrance of the river St. Lawrence, and so do the German surface craft that have attacked Canadian ships, both merchant ships
and ships of war, on the high seas. Further, if the axis powers should be victorious in this struggle, the people of Canada would very soon discover whether this is a Canadian war or merely an English war.
No; the imperialism, the lust for .power- military, economic, territorial-abides in the hearts of the axis rulers and nowhere else. It is they who began this war; it is they who have pursued it with a savage ferocity and brutality unknown since the days of the barbarians. It is they who took up the sword. It is they who will perish by the sword. And it is their leaders and those other men responsible for the atrocities that have been committed who must be brought to book and who will be brought to book in God's good time.
On our part and on the part of our allies this is a war of defence, defence against unprovoked aggression. Where that defence can best be carried out, where the enemy can be best met and subdued, is a matter that should be decided by those skilled in the art of war. This is Canada's war, and I believe that all Canadians are coming to realize this fact.
War is never a pleasant business. War always involves hardship and sacrifice and difficulty. In these grave times every man should speak his mind frankly and contribute whatever he can to the solution of the great problem now before us. I believe, as I said in the beginning, that this parliament should give to the government the power which it seeks, the power to apply conscription for overseas service, whenever the government thinks that step is necessary. I do not say that the moment is now or to-morrow or next week, but I do say that the moment may come, and may come suddenly. The government, in coming to its decision on that important point, will of course give every consideration to the needs of agriculture, to the needs of industry, and to the needs of Canadian defence. Let it never be thought that if this power is given to the government the result will be that every man in Canada will be hauled away overseas. No; we must maintain our farms; we must maintain our factories; we must maintain the defence of our own shores and our own soil.
But these things having been done, and there being still available some men for overseas sendee, and the need for conscripting these men having arisen, I say frankly that in my judgment the government should have the power to apply conscription. I say further that if it is demonstrated to the Canadian people that the need does exist, then those people will desire to have that need met.
3514	COMMONS
Mobilization Act-Mr. Macdonald (Kingston)
And when I say "the people of Canada" I mean all the people of Canada, and not the people of only certain parts of this country. I believe that when that need is seen and understood, Canada will meet it and still continue to be a united country. When our people realize that our existence as a nation is threatened, there is no Canadian who, seeing that condition, will not be willing to put forth every effort to meet it, and to meet it manfully.
I have only a moment more to speak, and in that time I wish to make one more reference. I remember that forty years ago Sir Wilfred Laurier some time after his return from a visit to England where he attended the Queen's Jubilee, made in the little Nova Scotia town of Arichat one of his most beautiful addresses. He said to those people-mostly French Acadians, sturdy loyal people as they were, have been and are- that when he was in Europe he had seen a beautiful cathedral. It was built of oak and marble and granite and glass, each of these elements retaining its own individuality and its own appearance, but each contributing its share to the beauty and symmetry of the whole. Then he went on to say, "That cathedral is the image of the nation I wish Canada to become. So long as I live," he said, "I shall repel the idea of changing the nature of any of the constituent elements of this country. I want the Englishman to remain the Englishman. I want the Irishman to remain the Irishman. I want the Scotsman to remain the Scotsman and the Frenchman to remain the Frenchman. But I want to take all these elements and weld them into a nation which will stand among the foremost nations of the world."
For myself, I adhere to Laurier's view; I hold to Laurier's vision. Let the races that people this country maintain their individuality; let them cling to their own traditions. But let there be running alongside of and in no way interfering with that loyalty to their own race, a loyalty to Canada, a willingness to defend Canada, a pride in the romantic and stirring story of her past, a hope for the bounty and beauty of her future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I express my thoughts on the important bill now before the house may I congratulate the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) upon the splendid speech he has just made. There was very little in that speech with which a member of His Majesty's loyal opposition could not heartily agree. I only wish the minister were

in the position of having associated with him in the cabinet, and behind him among the private members of his party, those who would give him the same support as he has here to-day in the ranks of the opposition.
To-day, Monday, June 22, 1942, is one of the grim days of a very grim war, because during the week-end the fortress of Tobruk has fallen, with the loss of 25,000 prisoners, and vast stores of equipment, including no doubt much equipment made in Canada. One cannot help thinking that if there had been Canadian troops with that Canadian equipment, this tragedy might not have occurred to the British empire and to the united nations. Further, during the week-end a wedge has been driven into the defences of our gallant Russian ally at Sevastopol. It looks to-day as though that great fortress, too, will fall within a very short time. To the west, out in the Aleutian islands the Japanese have taken their second stride toward our Pacific coast by seiziilg Kyska, some 270 miles nearer Dutch harbour than Attu, which they seized less than three weeks ago, and as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has said this afternoon, a Japanese submarine has shelled the Canadian coast at Estevan Point, halfway up the western coast of Vancouver island. This is the first time, I believe, in over a century that the shores of Canada have been under fire. I repeat: This is a grim day, and I hope the House of Commons will face the realities of the situation. I hope there will be less looking back, less reviewing things done decades or generations ago, less fanning the fires of old prejudices, and more facing of present day ugly facts, more looking fearlessly into the dark and yet challenging days ahead; less talk about national unity and more concern about national survival.
As hon. members are well aware, we are debating Bill No. 80, described as an act to amend the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940. This is a bill to repeal section 3 of that act, which section restricts the very wide powers of mobilization given the cabinet by section 2. It provides-and I quote from the section to be repealed:
The powers conferred by the next preceding section may not be exercised for the purpose of requiring persons to serve in the military, naval or air forces outside of Canada and the territorial waters thereof.
The provisions of that restriction have been narrowed to some extent by the government in that they have been taken as not applying to territory adjacent to Canada. I approve heartily of this bill and I shall vote for it. I believe it is necessary, and I believe also that it is very late. It should have been introduced into and passed by this house a

Mobilization Act-Mr. Green
long time ago. But I deplore the policy announced by the Prime Minister in connection therewith, which is in effect that although the restrictive section is to be repealed, the government will carry on as if the section were still in the act. We have been told and told quite clearly that the government believes that no change in policy is necessary yet, that it is merely removing this restriction in case the cabinet should decide that a change in policy is necessary at a later date, which later date the ministers have shown by their speeches during the present debate, they fervently hope will never come. Obviously the very thought of it gives them the jitters.
Apparently the Canadian cabinet believe that nothing has happened in the last few months to warrant a change in position. It makes one wonder whether they see the realities of the war at all. In recent months Great Britain has lost an army in Malaya, I believe the largest British army ever captured. Britain has lost thousands of men in Burma, and she has been forced to create a large new army in India. She has been forced to occupy Madagascar, and now she is planning to open a second front on the continent of Europe which will involve hundreds of thousands of men. Our Australian brothers have lost a division in Malaya, and they have been forced to recall their first-class fighting troops from the Mediterranean in order to protect their homeland against the Japanese. The United States have lost an army in the Philippines, the largest United States army ever captured. The Netherlands have lost their forces in the East Indies, and Russia has lost hundreds of thousands of her troops. Yet our cabinet believes that there has been no change in the situation in the last few months to justify any change in policy.
In actual fact the position to-day is that everyone in this house knows and the Canadian people at large know that we are not winning the war. It is a question whether we are holding our own. Let me warn the government that this is the time to throw in every ounce of our national strength without reservation. Let the cabinet do what is set out in the preamble of the National Resources Mobilization Act which confers upon the governor in council special emergency powers to permit of the mobilization of all the effective resources of the nation, both human and material. I warn the government further that a large majority of the Canadian people believe that the hour has come for all-out action, and called for such action by their vote on the plebiscite. In fact from the very start of the war the majority of the people in this country have been far ahead of the government in wanting to wage a total war.
This debate has drifted steadily away from the real issues brought forward by this bill, and I propose to state four of those issues as I see them. The main issue is not whether we are to have conscription, although one might think that that was so from the speeches that have been made in this debate. That issue was decided on June 21, 1940, when the National Resources Mobilization Act became law. There has been compulsion for over two years. The main issue now is whether men conscripted are to be available for service wherever they are needed. I repeat those words-wherever they are needed. They are not so available now, and will not be so long as the government continues its present policy. These men will be used only in Canada or in adjacent territories. That is the policy of the government at this present time. Unless they are needed to fight in or near Canada, they will never do any fighting. Minister after minister has risen in his place in the house during the present debate to emphasize the importance of keeping the enemy away from our shores; yet these young men serving under the terms of the National Resources Mobilization Act will have no part in keeping the enemy away from our shores. It may mean the waste of thousands of the cream of our young men by not making full use of them because they are tied down here in Canada under the present government policy. There can be no doubt that the present policy means that there is and that there will be no equality of sacrifice among our young men, because a young man may choose whether he will serve where he is needed or at home in Canada. I submit to the house that that is the main issue brought up by this bill.
Then there is a second issue-whether or not Canada is building up or can build up an efficient army in this country under the present government policy. Several ministers have placed a very low value as soldiers upon these young men called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act. I think that has been most unfair. Many of these men simply are not interested in the army because they consider it is the responsibility of the government to decide where they are to serve. In the meantime they are doing what they are ordered to do, in some cases with not a great deal of enthusiasm. Many of them have been under pressure from the time they were called up. Other young men who have seen fit to join the active forces receive extra leave, or considerations of one kind or another, such as being kept off fatigue duty. The men who will not join the active forces are not allowed to wear the badge "Canada" on their shoulders-
Mobilization Act-Mr. Green

The man who volunteers for the active army is allowed to wear this badge. I remember that in the last war nothing gave me more pride, nothing did more to raise my morale, than the fact that I had on my shoulder that badge "Canada." Yet under the present system these young men are not allowed to wear the badge of their country, and this will continue under the present government policy.
There are two types of troops in every unit except those that belong to the fourth division. The Prime Minister said in his speech the other day there were some 30,000 of these home defence troops and the number of these men who have not volunteered for service abroad will increase greatly from time to time.
That all means one thing, and one thing that is very serious; it means friction in the units in Canada. As a result it is difficult to have efficient units. As a result we are asking the commanders of these units to do the impossible. It is like asking a man to fight with one hand tied behind his back. I repeat that under this present policy we cannot build an efficient army in Canada.
The third real issue is whether or not *Canada is developing or can develop the spirit of the offensive, the will to wage war, without which there can be no victory. Under the present government policy we are developing a home defence complex. The talk, of which we had some this afternoon from the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald), is all to the effect that the place to fight the enemy is where you can find him, that the place to fight is beyond Canada. But that is not the government's policy under the National Resources Mobilization Act; the policy under that act is to build an army for Canada only, and the result is to focus the attention of the Canadian people on home defence when it should be on attack. Canada should be building here an army with which to strike out. For example, we should be building an army for the purpose of eventually striking out in the Pacific, perhaps into Alaska, perhaps to Siberia or Australia and finally into *Japan. This war will never be won on the north American continent unless it is won by the Germans and the Japanese.
The fourth and final real issue is whether or not the present policy is lowering the prestige of Canada, whether or not it is wounding the pride of the Canadian people in their nation-and probably this is the most serious issue of all. You know, it gives certain people the opportunity to rave -I use the word "rave" advisedly-about imperialism and colonialism and all that sort

of thing. This foolish talk, to which very few people here pay much attention, is apt to be taken seriously beyond our boundaries, and unfortunately this debate has brought out talk of that sort. It comes largely from the same people who talked the most and the hardest against Canada preparing for this war, who are mainly responsible for the tragic state of unpreparedness in which we found ourselves when war -broke out. The fact is, and this cannot be overemphasized too much, that the vast majority of the Canadian people in every province are proud to be in the British empire and intend to stay in it.
Then consider our relationship with the people of the United States, the great and friendly nation to the south. The American boy, under American policy, is called up and can be sent wherever he is needed, anywhere in the world-Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia; there is no limit. He goes where he is needed, and goes willingly. Under our present policy it is not so with the Canadian boy. It is very difficult to justify this to an American. The result of these differences in policy is that the American feels that Canada is not waging total war, and his Canadian friends feel deeply hurt by that attitude. Yet that is the position, and I do not think any hon. member of this house can deny it. Therefore I say that this policy is bad for Canada's prestige and bad for the national pride of our people.
In conclusion let me say again that these four issues are real; each is of vital importance, yet judged in the light of any one of them, the present policy of the government is wrong. That policy must be changed and changed quickly. It can never, never, never hold the respect or arouse the spirit of the Canadian people, because they are an intelligent, forthright, courageous people, and they know instinctively that it is a policy of doing things by halves. They know that the government is holding back. I urge upon the ministry, with all the force I can put into it, that they change their policy at once. If they do not feel that they can do so as a party ministry, let them set up a non-party government in this country. I urge them to lead the Canadian people from the present so-called "balanced .war effort"- and oh, how they gloat over those words!- into the only thing that really matters, and that is an all-out war effort. For it may be that only by so doing can our nation of Canada survive.

Mobilization Act-Mr. Maybank

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the last two speeches, and I wish to make only one comment with regard to what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) just before he sat down.
