Well, after what I might term this impetuous interruption, I must say that it is my intention to be perfectly frank, and I invite the same frankness from others. In what I have to say to-day I intend to speak with the utmost candour. I do not make remarks for the purpose of wounding any person, but simply to express the situation as I see it, and as I might talk about it personally with the hon. gentleman himself.
A few days ago I was struck by a remark or two made by the hon. gentleman who until a short time ago was ably bearing the burden of the portfolios of public works and transport. He adjured us at that time to be frank in all our dealings. I agree with him. We had a further reference to it this afternoon. I think candour is what we most need in all our dealings with each other. All of us have been guilty of saying less than the truth. I repeat that I do not wish by any sharp word or acid expression to injure or wound anyone. I would not be making any reference to the former minister with such an idea in mind, particularly in view of the fact that he is not
here this afternoon. We all know why he is not here; he is not a well man, and no doubt that accounts for his absence. I speak in no spirit of recrimination or in order to cast blame when I say that he himself, it seems to me, has been guilty in the past of some lack of candour. At the time the plebiscite vote was decided upon, the hon. gentleman had before him the whole vista which he can see to-day. He must have'known-at any rate he could have known-of the change of law which is now proposed. It does not seem to me that he made his position as clear then as he should have. However, in that regard lack of frankness is not to be found solely in that quarter. It has been evident over the last couple of years, this political lack of frankness, on the part of the government and of the various oppositions, and supporters of the government, among whom I include myself, and of the opposition parties. I do say that we have to get down to talking cold truth to each other. We must, to use Tennyson's words, "Cut prejudice against the grain."' In doing so, we need not forget that, "Gentle words are always gain."
The domestic history of Canada since the beginning of this war has been a striving after unity, and I do not think the government can be denied a great deal of praise for the degree of unity which has obtained in Canada ever since the war started. To some it seems as though the unity we have had thus far is to be destroyed. Personally I am entirely unwilling to subscribe to any such idea, but we have to look facts in the face in order to avoid disunity. It would appear that in the com troversy that is agitating Canada to-day there are eight provinces ranged on one side of the argument, with one province-old Quebec- standing alone on the other. Many people in parts of those eight provinces are angry with the people of the other province. Most of our colleagues who come from Quebec are opposed to the change in this law which can, and I think probably will, introduce the principle of compulsory service overseas. Most of Englishspeaking Canada is in favour of the law change, and, I believe, also in favour of the adoption of the compulsory service principle.
My views respecting compulsory service are well known. I favour the adoption of that principle, and in that respect I find myself in disagreement with my colleagues from the lower province. Further, when I think of the course the debate has taken, I confess to an impatience with the government itself, particularly in view of some of the remarks which have been made by supporters of the government. While such are my views, I should be sad indeed if any person supposed I have any-

Mobilization Act-Mr. Maybank
animus or any other feeling than deep affection not merely for all my colleagues from Quebec but for the people they represent. Some of my closest and dearest friends are those representatives. I have been the recipient of many services, many acts of friendship from them. Although my views as to what should be done in this matter may differ from theirs, I have no emotions other than amity and respect for all my colleagues from that part of Canada and for all the people of Quebec.
There may be small and unimportant groups in various parts of Canada where criticism of Quebec from time to time is rife. For my own part there never has been a time when I looked askance at the people of that province. None of my friends ever did, nor is it the usual thing in my community. I believe I have always had some appreciation of the difficulties of the Quebec situation. I remember a description of the people of Quebec which was given in this house by a Conservative member who is not now here; I refer to Mr. Heon, of Argenteuil. His remarks were a guide to me because I always felt that they were a pretty good description of the people of his province. I should like to read them to the house, because they lead to certain comments later. Speaking in the short war session, the hon. member said, as reported in Hansard of September 9, 1939, page 80:
May I now be allowed, on behalf of my own people, to make this urgent plea to my Euglish-Canadian friends? Never have I striven to be more sincere or convincing in all my life than in the appeal I am about to make. An immense majority of my compatriots have never concerned themselves with foreign affairs. They have never kept track of the sinuous courses of European diplomacy, nor have they taken time out to look up the meaning of "putsch" and "anschluss" or seek on a map of Europe the strategical value of Memel and Pomorze, Warsaw' and Lodz, Lauterbourg or the Saar basin.
The French Canadian has been mostly concerned, as were his ancestors before him, with clearing the forest, tilling the soil and providing food and shelter for the children with whom providence has blessed him from year to year. The practice of the golden rule, the presentation to the nation of stalwart intelligent sons and daughters, the defence of their territory against aggression, have been to my compatriots their main expressions of patriotism. The church, the little village, the large family, the soil enriched with their sw'eat, the peace and restfulness of the Quebec countryside, have drawn and kept their attention for three hundred years. The sons of French Canada have not been brought up in an atmosphere of militarism, nor have they spent their young days in playing with toy cannon and soldiers. Most of them have never shouldered a gun except to provide game for the family table. Very few' have ever had even elementary military training. It cannot be expected then that in three days -every one of them will be clamouring for a

one-way passage to the western front, or that, like some of us, their hearts will skip a beat at the mention of peace in Europe and the independence of Poland. Yet their honesty of purpose, their love of freedom, their devotion to Christian institutions, their loyalty to their king cannot be challenged. It may well be that ' this passionate love for their own land has somew'hat obscured the wider, the more international outlook on the W'elfare of mankind which W'e are now being asked to uphold and defend; but let me assure hon. members, that when Baptiste discovers that his freedom, institutions, and essential rights which he prizes so dearly are really threatened there will be no one w'ho will fight more savagely than he to defend them.
I wish to make just two comments on that passage. First I would remind hon. members that such a passage helps greatly or ought to help the Anglo-Saxon in apprehending the character and personality of the man of Quebec. The second comment I would make is that those who could have done it have not been making clear to these people the danger to the freedom, insititutions and essential rights which are prized so dearly, as Heon says. I desire a little later to come back to that passage, but just at the moment I wish to move on to other matters for the purpose of indicating to the house the disquietude to which I referred a little while ago, and the reasons for it.
What is disquieting to me about this law and the debate upon it is the nature of the statements that are being made. One statement seems to suggest that the law is being amended for a purpose, that it is being amended for use, and another statement seems to suggest that it is not being amended for any purpose at all and will never be used, and that there is no occasion for using it. I feel that at this time the government could be much more simple and direct than it has been thus far. I know you cannot have the government name the date on which a certain act or policy will be put into force, but it does seem to me that we could do better than have speeches one day which indicate the utter improbability of the law ever being used, and another day the distinct probability that it will be used. I notice with considerable disquietude certain statements that have been made. Take this for instance. It is said that compulsory service for overseas is not necessary and that reinforcement needs are already well in hand. To my way of thinking, to base any policy upon a statement of that kind is not wise. That is a quite unimportant statement. Reinforcement needs are apparently about 1J per cent. When one says the situation is well in hand for the army, then by implication one is saying that there will be no change in the army's

position. It means that a second front is eyewash. It means there will not be any attempted invasion, or if there is, it will be in a place where Canadian soldiers are not. Or perhaps it means that if there is a second front they will not be there. It seems to me that to lay plans on any such assumptions as these is unwise. I think that such assumptions themselves are invalid.
Reference has already been made to the present situation of our army. At the present time no person can deny, I am sure the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) will not deny, that we have an illogical and unsystematic condition in the army. Volunteers and draftees are called in together. If reinforcements are demanded, the odds have to be separated from the evens, the V's from the D's, and if a large reinforcement draft is needed it cannot be got from one place. Reinforcement drafts have first of all to be picked out from here and there, and pieced together afterwards. If there is virtue in men working together, it is lost under that system. It does not seem to be good business. It may be necessary; it may be that we shall never get away from it. I should like to see a definite statement on the question as to probabilities.
I believe a change from that sort of thing is inevitable, and if it is inevitable we might as well face it, although perhaps it is not necessary to-morrow morning. I do not say it is. I believe that what should be done is to indicate the probability now in order that people may become accustomed to it.
Now, upon the general question of necessity for compulsory service, I believe that has not been the test in the past. No person, for example, would say that compulsory service was instituted for Canada upon the grounds of necessity. It is patently absurd to say that conscription for overseas service is not necessary, that volunteers will do, that there are plenty of volunteers, but that when it comes to defence of the hearth and the home on this very soil, resort must be had to compulsion. Obviously we never instituted compulsory service in this country with any such idea in mind. When men were called for thirty days training we did not call them with the idea of forming a defence-of-Canada army; that was patently absurd also. We called them up for other reasons, partly I think in order to get the principle of compulsory service accepted and to get the people accustomed to it. That was what I believed at the time, and I blame myself for not having said so. Likewise, when it was extended to four months, that was not done with the intention of forming an army for the defence of Canada, nor yet again when the men were continued for the duration of
Mobilization Act-Mr. Maybank
the war was it for the defence of Canada. We have never had compulsory service in Canada with that idea in mind.
If anyone has any doubt whatever about that proposition I ask him to consider three points. The first is that we never expected a military attack from the east. The second is that we did not expect a war with Japan, and consequently we did not expect an attack on the west coast. Since these propositions are true, obviously we were not creating an army for the defence of Canada. But if these reasons are not enough to convince one that the draft was not for the defence of Canada, there is a third reason which settles the point conclusively. This third reason is that we took no steps to equip the army for combat under modern warfare conditions, and I doubt very much whether we are doing so yet. No; we decided long ago in favour of compulsory service for overseas, but the manner of doing it was to institute compulsory service at home with the object of getting recruits in the overseas forces.
There cannot be any doubt about that.
I think we ought to be perfectly frank with each other. Now another statement is made, which to say the least, is disturbing. It has already been dealt with this afternoon by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs (Mr. Macdonald), with whose views I agree. The statement is that men brought into the army as draftees do not make good soldiers. Why this should be said I do not know. I think sometimes people say it simply to make a point, to win an argument. There has not been any Canadian or world experience to support it. So far as the last war was concerned, the time was too short, and the circumstances under which the policy was instituted were such as pretty well to vitiate that experience as an example to use in coming to a conclusion. Most of the armies in the last war were composed of draftees. I remember reading Lloyd George's comment on the defence of Verdun-all by draftees. I think it is generally admitted that that was the greatest defence ever put up in the long history of warfare in the world up to that time. And again we have only to mention Dunkirk, Libya, Crete, Greece, in regard to British military service, and Moscow with reference to Russia; and Bataan might be added in order to show that there is no natural inferiority in men who are called up. Of course if you wait until you have a large percentage of thoroughly unwilling people, then you may have a bad soldier through the draft, but it is not native to the case itself.

Mobilization Act-Mr. May bank
I	mention Bataan. I think the fact is that at Bataan there were some United States volunteers and some draftees; but that they were all heroes no one would for a moment deny. There you had draftees mixed with volunteers, so that the difficulty referred to by some, I think by the Prime Minister himself, about mixing	one	kind	with	another,does not hold, at any rate does not always hold. I do not doubt that the people of Britain are resting a great deal easier by reason of the fact that they have there a fine volunteer army from Canada. I do not doubt, either,	that	they	rest	easy by
reason of the fact that, in addition, they now have a large United States draftee army.
I have no doubt that they feel just about as well pleased with the one as with the other.
Let me make one other comment on that subject. Some of	those	who	say	that thedraftee will not make a	good	soldier forget
that they are practically sending a cable to the axis to this effect: "If, as, and when Canada undertakes to raise soldiers in that way, do not worry; she will only be introducing second-rate men. Well, it strikes me rather like crying "stinking fish" on one's own doorstep.
I began by referring to the difficulty in this country by reason of the division of eight and one. I have a practical proposal to make to the government, and I make it in all sincerity and with emphasis. I said that I thought we had not been as frank as we might have been. I take my share of the blame in that regard. I do not think we have been always as frank with the people -of Canada as we might have been, nor have we looked to the people of Canada for help as we should have. I can quite understand the difficulty, almost insuperable at the moment, which faces the government, but that difficulty will have to be surmounted. The change will have to be made; the logic of events is forcing it. I would say that if the government feel they cannot follow the course which pure reason dictates, they should go direct to the common law provinces and say to them in simple and direct language, that, because of many historical facts, because of differences in education and environment, the lower province is not yet ready to go along with the rest of Canada in the plan which seems to be most reasonable and would appear to be most efficient. It would be right to say to the people of the common law provinces that the people of old Quebec have done much more than has ever been realized by Anglo-Saxon Canadians, and to show what those things have been.

The former minister of transport (Mr. Cardin) was quite right when he said that satisfactory figures on French-Canadian enlistment have never been given. I say, do not present the difficulty with a whole lot of statistics and involved arguments; you can prove almost anything with figures. It would not have been at all difficult at the beginning of this war to prove conclusively by statistics that we could not possibly accomplish half of what we have actually accomplished up to this time. At the beginning it could have been shown that if we sent 100,000 men overseas it was about all we could do if we were to make munitions in any large way. I say, do not go to the people in that way. Make them see that the French Canadians for three hundred years have been engaged in clearing the forests and tilling the soil and raising children and practising the golden rule with their neighbours rather than in acquiring an international outlook. Present these facts-to the people of the common law provinces and tell them you want more time because of these difficulties. I do not guarantee success with this plan, but I think the government would get somewhere with it. The recommendation should not be dismissed too lightly. The very novelty of it should make it attractive, because such frankness has never been tried in the world by any government. No harm can come from the Canadian people to any government as a consequence of their being simple, straightforward and honest.
But do not stop there. That is not the place to stop. Turn to Quebec; put the problem into the hands, of the people there. The method might have to be different; probably it would. We all know this is no imperialistic war, but it seems from what has been said here that there are some men in the lower province who are not fully convinced of that fact. We know that everything that is being done is being done for the defence of Canada, and it is necessary to bring that home to all our fellow Canadians, including those in that province as well. Make them appreciate that there is no imperialism about this war, but that it is solely a war for the defence of Canada. Let this be brought home to every village and farm. What would be necessary would be the carrying on of a campaign of truthful, virile, systematic and emphatic education throughout the province. The Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) strikes me as being just about the man for the job. I am convinced that if the people of his province could have heard and seen him as he spoke, there would be no doubt of their being convinced as to the serious predicament in which we find ourselves.

Mobilization Act-Mr. Mcllraith
In other words, what is necessary there is the achievement of that which I read this afternoon. Hon. members will recall this passage: Let me assure hon. members that y4ien Baptiste discovers that his freedom, institutions, and essential rights which he prizes so dearly are really threatened, there will be no one who *will fight more savagely than he to defend them.
This is the point that needs to be brought home. The difficulties of the situation with respect to Quebec have to be made known to the people of all the provinces, and there is a hope for a continuance of the unity of races in Canada if a policy of candour something along these lines be adopted.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OP SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks I should like to congratulate the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) upon his speech of this afternoon. Both as to clarity of expression and *quality of content it seemed to me outstanding, and will, I believe, serve a useful purpose not only within but outside the house.
In adequately discussing the subject before the house to-day it seems to me some difficulty arises by reason of the fact that two of the major considerations entering into any decision lie peculiarly within the knowledge of the government. To arrive at a proper conclusion in the matter one would need to know more adequately, and, indeed, would desire to know more adequately the programme of the united nations as a whole. One would need to know the relative programmes of each of the united nations, and their requirements of men and munitions. In addition, one would need to know not only Canada's munitions programme, which is generally known throughout the country, but the programme with respect to and the nature of any projected military operations.
Those are matters which for obvious reasons cannot be made known to the public at large, or, indeed, to individual members of the house. For these reasons, in conducting a full or adequate discussion of the amendment to the National Resources Mobilization Act we are handicapped, and allowances must be made accordingly. The result of the present procedure in dealing with this measure is that we are now having a full discussion of the subject of conscription for overseas service. In addition, not only do we have that discussion now, but we have it only once- not repeated, as some would have it. In my opinion, the decision to have the debate only once is one which will commend itself to all hon. members and to Canadians
generally. It commends itself not only because the time at which a measure of conscription may become necessary is something peculiarly within the knowledge of the government, but also because of the bitterness and the opening of old sores which any argument on the subject engenders. I must confess frankly that at times I have found myself unable to understand the bitterness and prejudices which rear their heads when this subject is mentioned. I was too young to remember the time when those prejudices originated, but I have lived to regret that they were ever created or permitted to exist.
On the one hand, to-day we have those who oppose conscription for military service overseas saying that the hands of the government should be tied, that Bill No. 80 is a conscription measure and that because they feel conscription for overseas is mot now necessary, we should not free the hands of the government. It seems to me that this argument completely ignores the element of speed in the changing military situation. In ignoring that element and leaving the hands of the government tied, the persons who would follow this procedure place themselves in a most dangerous position.
It is well known that there can be some delay in taking action of this kind by legislative action. Surely, when time after time in the last two years, and particularly in the last week, it has been demonstrated that the whole military picture can change with a rapidity which is positively startling, the government should have a free hand. For that, among other reasons, I for one most wholeheartedly support the bill now before the house.
On the other hand, there is another group in the community who say not only that we should have conscription for military service overseas, but that we should have it now. And not only that; they reinforce their argument by saying that an affirmative vote on the plebiscite was a vote for conscription. It may be true that the majority of those persons who voted in the affirmative voted that way because they believed in conscription for overseas service. It is equally true, however, that a very large number voted in the affirmative, not because they believed that conscription for overseas service at the present time was a proper measure, but because they desired the government to be free. They felt that the question asked meant precisely what it says. Taking a serious view of the war, they felt that notwithstanding their anti-conscription feelings of the moment they should free the hands of the government and leave it in a position

Mobilization Act-Mr. Mcllraith
all parties in this house and did not encounter any opposition from any section of the community except with regard to military service overseas, it seemed to me that it should be used and used at once with respect to these reserve brigade groups. To my disappointment I find that this has not been done. I have not the exact figures to give the house at the moment with regard to the strength of these reserve brigade groups, but perhaps I can convey some idea of the situation when I say that the strength of these groups is equal to about four divisions. So it will be seen that it is a rather sizable and important item in our defence scheme. It will be seen as well that it would be of importance also in releasing some men, full-time soldiers, for service elsewhere when they might be needed. I, for one, hold the view that the place to defeat the enemy is as far from our shores as we can meet him.
I have some knowledge of the reserve brigade group in this military district, No. 3. The strength of the group should be approximately 6,400. The actual strength some two weeks ago was about 2,700. Some 3,700 recruits were required to bring it up to strength. In other words, this reserve brigade group is something less than one-half the strength it should be. If this force, which should equal about four divisions, should be called out in case of an attempted invasion, the necessity would arise very quickly. It would come like a whirlwind, and there would be no time to train men. Then, instead of having a force of some four divisions, are we to go out with an actual strength of some two divisions and say to the enemy attempting to invade our shores, "We have other men in Canada who have been kept at civilian work because they were doing necessary war work. We did not give them any military training. This force now meeting you should have the strength of four divisions, but it has only the strength of two divisions." That position, of course, would be absolutely absurd; yet in our treatment of this subject, while looking at the more important and more distant matter, having the old war mentality, we have completely overlooked a smaller, supplementary matter right at hand. The reserve brigade groups should be brought up to strength by the use of the National Resources Mobilization Act. The necessity for taking such action I think has been clearly shown in recent weeks by the visit of enemy submarines to the mouth of the St. Lawrence. Those submarines were not there on any friendly mission, nor were the Japanese on the west coast there for any nonsense. As far as I am concerned, we should have no illusions as to why they were there, or as to what we may expect in future.

The policy of the government with respect to the matter is clear. The principle of this act has been accepted and enforced. Not only that, but in his address on June 10 the Prime Minister had this to say, as reported at page 3241 of Hansard:
And make no mistake about it, the government is determined, as far as is humanly possible, to make sure that every able-bodied man undertakes some form of direct war service.
Here is a form of direct war service suitable to the able-bodied men who have been retained in civilian occupations. The administrative machinery to put it in force is in existence, but as yet our military authorities have not put it in force. I respectfully submit, Mr. Speaker, that the time has come to put it in force, and that the time is now. I do not believe our views on the matter should be obscured by any other views with respect to the major, more important part of our army, the active part, or any views that we may hold with regard to conscription for military service overseas.
In closing, in view of the fact that I have not been inclined to say a great deal in this house, I should like to point out that the constituency I have the honour to represent has more than nine units on active service for overseas. That is a record which, I believe, not only has not been equalled but has not been approached in any other part of Canada. This representation of the active forces from my constituency, of which I am very proud, typifies, I believe, better than anything I could say the views of the people I represent with respect to the war and matters pertaining to it.
Mrs. CORA T. CASSELMAN (Edmonton East): Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations on Bill No. 80. I have listened with pleasure and profit to speeches made by hon. members in this house, and have agreed with a great deal and disagreed with some things that have been said. I was particularly interested in the statements of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and members of his cabinet, setting out the case as they see it at the present time. Sometimes I think that the men who bear the burden and heat of the fray do not receive sufficient praise for what they do, for it must take tremendous courage, initiative, perseverance and patience to carry on at this time.
We see the war becoming more and more dangerous. It will be won finally by the young men and women of the belligerent countries fighting either on their own soil, within their own boundaries, or outside. I hope and pray that it will be won by the youth of our

Mobilization Act-Mrs. Casselman
own allied countries, fighting beyond our borders. I hope it will never come so close that we have to fight on Canadian soil.
There is an urgency now for Canada's sake. There is an urgency for the sake of our allies and for humanity's sake. How can we look at our young people here, so free and gay and fair, without thinking of the young people of the occupied countries of Europe and Asia sitting in darkness and the shadow of death? It is bad enough for us to see our people in uniform ready for the conflict. How much worse it must be for these others to see their fellow citizens, civilians, young and old, in danger from the ever-present and ever-vigilant enemy; how much harder still to witness the outrages, the massacres, the executions and the bombings, even to read of which makes our blood run cold. Therefore there is need for haste; we must set aside all differences which may impede the war effort.
Conditions have changed a great deal since the war began. At first the United States hoped to stay out, and Canada believed that no more than limited participation would be necessary. But world events have forced on us a greater and greater participation in this struggle. I think our yardstick should be, not what others are doing but what I myself am doing, in fighting or working or saving; not what somebody else is doing in another province or another community but what we ourselves are doing to contribute to the success of the war measures. If we put it on that ground; if we are driven by that urgency, we see that the inexorable pressure of world events have made it necessary to advance step by step along this line of participation which has been deplored by some hon. members who have spoken in this house. Not politics, not something else, but world events have forced this condition upon us. There has been a tremendous change. In the beginning it was thought that the war would be one of machines, with comparatively few men engaged. But more and more men have been called. The geographical area has extended vastly, and with savagery and brutality the enemy have made those of the occupied lands work for them on factories and on farms, freeing millions of their own men for the battle front.
These are the considerations which have forced us in the direction of greater participation in the war effort. Some there are who do not want to free the government, who would not give it power to increase its effort and to put more men in the field should this become necessary. I cannot see the justification for that attitude so long as we are a 44561-223
democracy. This is our own government. It is the decisions which our government will take which will involve greater participation if and when it becomes necessary. One of the reasons why Canada is at war is to preserve our right to make our own decisions, to maintain our democratic ways of life, and surely it is the democratic spirit which inspires the discussion we are now holding; for policy is hammered out by the meeting of many minds. Discussion precedes decision, which is followed by loyal support and then by action to carry out those decisions. We thus preserve our right to make decisions.
We all build Canada: those in the field; those here at home, in the factory, and on the farm and in the home. But it is not what we have contributed, valuable though that may be; it is not entirely what was done in past years; it is what we do now which builds Canada of the present and the future; for all our to-morrows are built on to-day. Each part of the country shares in the government; its constitutional rights are set out in the British North America Act. Individuals, too, have their rights, not necessarily set down in the constitution, but exercised by the ability they can display, through what they themselves can contribute. The men who are here in the house representing different parties are here partly because they kept Canada as Canada in the great war. The hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. Warren) has listed the names of some of the men who served in the great war and who, because of that service, are here now. He might have named many more. The men of 1942 are earning their right, now and for the future, to build Canada. For example, I have here an enumeration of honours in the king's birthday list, and I find the names of three Edmonton fliers who have won distinctions. Two of them are mentioned in dispatches-Flight-Sergeant R. J. Majeau and Flight-Sergeant P. A. Rogers. We can tell from their names something of their racial extraction. Also Sergeant E. Gowda has won the British Empire Medal. I should like to read briefly from the newspaper account:
Sergeant Gowda was awarded the Empire Medal for work contributing to the efficiency of his squadron and for "great gallantry" in extricating companions from a crashed, burning plane while with an eastcoast bomber squadron.
Sergeant Gowda is a Canadian of Ukrainian extraction, the second generation, I believe. I know his mother well. The best of every race, French, British and new Canadian stock, are taking their part in the present conflict and earning their right to build up Canada now and in the future. I hope, therefore, for unity; I hope that we shall set aside those



Mobilization Act-Mrs. Casselman
divisions which may exist among us and that we shall have the privilege of building Canada one in soul and strength and sword. Furthermore, I think those very principles that we carry out here in our national government, the principles of democracy, discussion, decision, support and action, are the principles that must underlie any international organization which may be built up at the end of this war if we are to save the world from a recurrence of wars such as this. It seems to me that therein lies our hope for a world free from the ever-recurring curse of war. We survived one war and we hope to survive this one; but can civilization survive a succession of wars that bleed it white? Canada must play her part in the war and in the peace that will follow, in whatever organization seems best fitted to carry out the policies that we ourselves put into force here in our own country; for it seems to me that these democratic principles are what will have to be carried out on a world scale if we are to avoid such a conflagration again.
Fifty per cent of my reading during the last thirty years has been along this line. It is something to which I have given a great deal of consideration, because I, too, lived and worked and thought through the last war. The problem has to be worked out together in some way, just as we ourselves in Canada must work out our lesser problems. It will need a combination of effort, and we see at the present time the allies getting together and outlining their policies for the post-war period. We see this in the treaties that have been signed between Russia and Great Britain and in the attitude of the united nations as indicated in the Atlantic charter and the agreement of the twenty-six nations signed early this year. The future is already taking shape, and our policies will have to be hammered out just as we hammer out our policies here where we hear the noise of the hammer and the din of conflict of opinion, the decisions that are taken, the support given and the action following. Canada then may show the way, by her policy here at home, whereby a world organization can live and survive with better success than the League of Nations did twenty years ago. Of course, it will depend on the individual members of any league.
I love Canada instinctively, as the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) said, but I love Canada with the head as well as the heart. I love Canada because here we have a country in which we work out the principles of decent equality between men, a country in which we have the four

freedoms, not 100 per cent, though the tendency is in that direction more and more as the years go by. I love Canada for its history. I believe I have taken as much pride and pleasure in the history of French Canada as any French Canadian, and I was taught in Ontario schools, where the history of Canada included not only British history but French Canadian history as well. I believe I have as much pride as anyone in Frhnch Canada. The history of Canada for me began when the first French explorer placed his foot on Canadian soil. Those explorers were to me heroes as they were to French Canadians-Madeleine de Vercheres, Father Breboeuf, Dollard, LaFontaine, Laurier and others coming down to our own times. So that Canada means a great deal to me even though perhaps we have not had the centuries on the soil that the French Canadians have had. Again, I love Canada because she has learned to live in peace with her neighbours. I love her because of her undefended boundary line, because on both sides of that line we have had the frame of mind that allows people to live in peace. We have approached the consideration of our problems without prejudice; we have hammered out our policies, and have stood by our decisions, and so we have avoided war along the boundary.
I love Canada also because it is the world in miniature. In Canada there is no single blood or race or religion, but a combination of all these; and therefore, as it works out its internal problems, it shows how the external problems of the world can be worked out. It would be a great pity if anything happened now to destroy that sense of unity, that sense of oneness which we have right across Canada. As the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe said, we have two languages and one soul. In fact, we have more than two languages. We have English and French and we have the new Canadians of different stock, but we have one soul throughout Canada. Therefore I vote for this measure, willingly giving to the government the power it needs, to use that power as it sees fit, when and if it is necessary; for a government without power is no government. It is anarchy. I hope that out of these troubled waters Canada will emerge stronger, one in soul and strength and sword.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OP SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with apprehension that I rise to address the house on this very important bill, No. 80, first, because I am a new member, and second, because I have decided to speak in the language of the majority of this house. If I dare to speak in your language, Mr. Speaker,

Mobilization Act-Mr. Fauteux
in spite of the fact that my vocabulary is poor and my pronunciation inadequate, it is because I wish to pay a tribute of gratitude and of admiration to the English-speaking members who have been so kind and generous toward the province of Quebec in the speeches they have delivered.
It is not my intention to analyse all that has been said in the house for or against the bill, or to analyse the bill itself. My intention is simply to say how I shall vote and why, and to make a few suggestions.
The government has already said that if this bill has been introduced it is simply to comply with the wish expressed by the majority of the Canadian people through the plebiscite, namely, to release the government from the promises which they or any members of this house may have made to their electors, with regard to the mobilization of man-power, during the election of 1940, when the military situation was absolutely different from the one that exists to-day. If we had that plebiscite it was because the government felt that during this war, when we are fighting for a principle like the sanctity of treaties and contracts, we should at least hold to our own promises made to the people of Canada. The great majority of the people having voted "yes" on the plebiscite, the government feels obliged to abrogate section 3 of the mobilization act in order to have no restriction on the mobilization of man-power.
In a few hours or a few days we shall have to vote "yes" or "no" on the motion for the second reading of this bill. What am I going to do? How am I going to vote if I believe in the democratic form of government, in a government of the people, for the people, and by the people, and if, like the government I believe in the sanctity of treaties and contracts? I do not need to go back as far as 1940; I have only to refer to February last during the by-election, when I asked 50,000 electors of St. Mary to place a contract with me, a contract that has since been accepted and executed by the party of the first part representing the majority of the electors of Montreal-St. Mary, in electing me and the party of the second part, the one who is called to execute the condition sine qua non of the contract, with the mandate that has been given to him by the party of the first part.
What was the important clause for which I was responsible in that contract? Let me read just a few lines of an article written in the newspaper La Presse of Montreal under date of April 30 and signed by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot):
(Translation)
Their new member, who was supported by a majority of people who were surely against 44561-223^
conscription, has of course, stated his opposition to conscription for overseas service. But he has bound himself to vote against the plebiscite not in the House of Commons, as the member for Saint Mary, but only as a citizen, as an elector of the constituency of Westmount. The electors will no doubt be interested to know what he will do if a conscription measure is ever introduced in the house. We will make it a point to keep them informed.
In a few words, all that means is that the hon. member for St. Mary promised to his electors during the last election to vote for a plebiscite when it would be introduced in this house by the government, but that he would vote "no" as an individual whenever the plebiscite would be held. The hon. member for Temiscouata said, "I wonder what the new member will say when he will have to vote 'yes' or 'no' on conscription when conscription is introduced in the house." Let me tell this house that I will carry out my engagement and that I will vote against this bill. To my hon. friends who may be scandalized by that clause in my contract with my electors or inclined to call that demagogy, whether they be Liberals who will vote for the bill, to be logical with their attitude on the plebiscite, or whether they be Tories with imperialistic instincts, let me tell them immediately that I am not and never was a narrow-minded nationalist or separatist. Let me ask them if they would have preferred to have in this house, instead of a true democrat and a Liberal, who believes that this war is Canada's war, who is glad and proud to belong to a country privileged to have two civilizations, which I hope will remain united in one soul, and one who has three children, all of them in English schools in order to become perfectly bilingual and true Canadians, an extremist like the one who ran against me as a candidate for the party "a sens unique" of the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe).
Let me ask the right hon. the Prime Minister and hon. members of this house not to blame the electors of my county, the same people who voted for Mr. Camillien Houde as mayor of Montreal, and elected him as their representative in the legislative assembly of Quebec, the same who is now in a concentration camp, whom they used to consider their "lucky boy", if they asked their candidate to be against conscription, but praise them because at the same time they refused to send to the parliament of Canada an extremist. I am really convinced that they believe in that latin phrase, in medio stat virtue. This does not mean that they want only a moderate effort in this war. No. They want, like all of us, to win the war, and they will do everything possible for the defence of Canada.
Mobilization Act-Mr. Fauteux

Let me read what Professor F. R. Scott of McGill university said about the province of Quebec, which would apply also to my constituency:
The French Canadians mean what they say when they say they will do everything necessary for the defence of Canada. They have already accepted conscription of man-power for this purpose, and they do not mind whether this means going to Alaska, Greenland or Panama. It is a good deal farther from Quebec city to Alaska than from Quebec city to London.
Further on he says:
The same people who voted "no" so overwhelmingly in Mr. St. Laurent's constituency, only a short time ago preferred Mr. St. Laurent to a nationalist candidate who posed as the de Valera of Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OP SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at six
o'clock I had just given some reasons why Quebec is against conscription for overseas service. I may point out that those were only some among many reasons why they are opposed. The main one is that, like most of us, they believe it is not necessary, and that total war effort does not necessarily mean conscription for overseas service. They think they are right, like most of us; and I may say that both of us are in good company with Australia, South Africa and Northern Ireland.
The people of Quebec believe in a total war effort to win the war. They have listened to Mr. Churchill and have applauded his courage and determination. They have listened to the fireside chats of Mr. Roosevelt, and they are not only ready to let their sons join the army voluntarily for overseas service, but to answer to the demand of Mr. Churchill, "Give us the tools and we will finish the job," and approve Mr. Roosevelt's statement that America-and that means Canada and the United States

is the arsenal of democracy. Yes; let us give tools to Mr. Churchill. Let us ask our people to work night and day to produce tools to avoid more defeats like Greece, Crete, Singapore, Hong Kong and Libya.
What we should do for a total war effort is to keep Canada as a real arsenal of democracy for the nations who fight with us, nations which

have large populations but have not the industrial strength of the United States and Canada. I said a real arsenal, because we need tools for that unfortunate China with her 420,000,000 inhabitants; tools for that gallant Russia with her 120,000,000 inhabitants; tools for that unhappy Poland with her 32,000,000 inhabitants, and tools for those millions of inhabitants of the northern part of Europe, as well as those in the centre, who are only waiting for the right moment to be armed and to start a revolution.
We need tools-tools and all kinds of armaments for land, air and sea, in order that those heroic British and Canadian commandos, and de Gaulle and his gallant free Frenchmen may land on the soil of France, to hand those tools to the people of France; tools with which they will be able to invade and conquer the European continent, tools to destroy the beasts, both the one which invaded her soil, killed her sons and destroyed her monuments, and the other which stabbed her in the back during her agony; and, finally, tools for our beloved Canada. Yes; tools for our shores on the Atlantic and on the Pacific, to protect and keep our beloved land colonized by France, so well developed by Britain, and transformed into a nation by our Canadian statesmen.
I believe that in order to do that we do not need to abrogate section 3. The government has only to exercise the power given it under the National Resources Mobilization Act to get more money by the following means:
1.	By nationalizing the war industries for the duration, with the understanding that a reasonable interest will be paid, and a reasonable power of amortization will be given.
2.	By mobilizing all the savings frozen since 1939, with the understanding that a reasonable interest will be paid.
3.	By establishing a reasonable ceiling for annual revenues of the individual, the remainder being remitted to the government.
In offering these suggestions, I humbly believe that if they were accepted Canada would make a total war effort in a spirit of total national unity. That, in my opinion, is the best way to win the war, to win the peace, and to assure the future of our country. In doing so, we shall confirm what has already been said by Mr. Graham Spry, former secretary of the Association of Canadian Clubs: "One nation, two cultures; one loyalty, two races; two glorious pasts but only one future."

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OP SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the time at my disposal to-night I assume the very serious responsibility of expressing myself in a language which is not my mother tongue, one which I must confess I am far from mastering. I wish to pay tribute in their own

Mobilization Act-Mr. Cote
language to the spirit of good-will and understanding of the English-speaking citizens in the constituency which I have the honour to represent. I shall also speak in this language with a certain amount of pride and pleasure, because it will enable me to address myself in a direct, if not a perfect way to my colleagues of British descent in the house, and to tell them most sincerely how much I have appreciated the friendships with which they have honoured me during the two years I have sat in this chamber.
In passing, I wish to point, with great pride as a Canadian and with no less hope for the future of Canada, to their sincere attempts to approach and to discuss in a comprehensive and courteous manner the internal difficulties our country has not been spared in this critical day. The better I have come to know my colleagues, the more I have appreciated them. I realize that there is one main condition which must be met before complete and lasting unity is achieved in this country. There must be a better knowledge of each other's history, traditions and ideals in order to justify our claim to true citizenship in this country. True Canadians must love not only the soil of their country but also the inhabitants of that soil, irrespective of their racial beliefs; they must respect the institutions which regulate each other's social, religious and political life.
Such a result cannot be achieved in a short period of time. Canada has a population of only 11,500,000 people, but its area is equal to the whole of Europe or to the United States with its territorial possessions. As with a human being, the impulse of life of a nation must come from the heart. Ottawa, the capital city, where meet the representatives from all the provinces, is the heart of Canada. Therefore we as members have a definite responsibility to discharge in furthering national unity. We must take back to our constituents a better picture of the other parts of Canada which most of them have never visited, and of the people living in those different districts. In my province there are villages and even municipalities peopled with those of French descent which seldom see visitors of any other extraction. Is it any wonder that my compatriots have such a vague knowledge of their fellow citizens in other parts of Canada and that campaigns of prejudice led by extremists of all sorts result in discontent and mistrust.
I am told by my colleagues from other provinces that the same situation exists in their constituencies. A great number of citizens there have never met a French Canadian, and the only knowledge they have of French Canadians is from the newspapers. If the
one they happen to read is of the type whose supreme ambition is to disunite the country, one should not be astonished at the bad feeling that arises from time to time between the different races whose destiny it is to build a strong and prosperous nation. The main and vital link between the two racial groups in our dominion must be forged here in Ottawa by the members of this house. If they discharge that duty as they should, the cornerstone of national unity will be laid and will last forever.
On April 27 the dominion government asked the population of this country to release it from past pledges. The question was in the following form:
Are you in favour of releasing the government from any obligation arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service?
This was a special occasion indeed. The public was invited to take a direct share of the responsibility of administering the affairs of this country. It was with that thought in mind that I approved the principle of the plebiscite, as will be seen from my remarks made in the house on February 12. Nevertheless, the question was ambiguous, and the members of this government have been the first to admit that. Perhaps that fact has accounted for the great number of those who developed that particular theme during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, as well as those who repeatedly addressed the public over the radio and through the newspapers during the few weeks which preceded the vote when an effort was made to explain the true meaning of the question and predict the results of an affirmative or a negative vote.
On February 12, when I addressed the house for the first time, I supported the policy of the government in connection with this plebiscite. I considered that policy to be a most democratic procedure and I did not hesitate to endorse its principles. Following the magnificent speech delivered by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) over the radio on April 7, I went to my constituency and opened a campaign in favour of an affirmative vote. I appealed to my fellow citizens to release me from the pledge which I had given during the last election campaign and which I had repeated on several occasions afterwards. Following the worthy speeches which had been made across the country by outstanding members of this house, I promised my constituents that conscription was not directly related to the issue of the plebiscite. I asserted that an affirmative vote would not be a vote in
Mobilization Act-Mr. Cote

favour of conscription. I gave them to understand that the circumstances of this war were such that it had become necessary and imperative in order to maintain the unity of the country that members of parliament be released from any past commitments made with regard to the method of raising men for overseas service.
I told my constituents that parliament should be allowed to consider any appropriate measure without any restriction, should be completely free to act if circumstances developed which made it necessary to bring in such a measure for the furtherance of our war effort. I was greatly honoured on the evening of April 27 to learn that my constituents had listened to my plea and had responded to the call of the Prime Minister. They had given a majority of over 8,600 affirmative votes. That meant that two-thirds of the total vote of my constituency was affirmative. During my first speech in this house I said that the constituency of Verdun seemed to me to be a miniature Canada because of the various racial and religious groups to be found there. The result of the plebiscite would seem to confirm that statement because the final returns for the whole country showed the same two-thirds majority in the affirmative.
The plebiscite was held with a view to learning the will of the people concerning the pledges which had been made and which prevented the government and the members of this house from having a free hand in carrying out our war effort. It is most important that a correct interpretation should be given to the results of the plebiscite. As far as I am concerned as the representative of Verdun, I consider myself released from the obligations I had assumed in the past when I promised my constituents that I would never favour conscription, that I would oppose any bill which would bring in conscription for overseas service. Moreover, in view of the appeal I made for an affirmative vote in the plebiscite campaign and the interpretation which was generally given to the statements made over the radio and through the press by outstanding members of this house who took a very active part in the campaign, I am bound to consider that the will of the majority in Verdun has given me a special mandate to withhold from debating conscription until such circumstances have arisen as would render it necessary for the furtherance of our total war effort. If such events should present themselves, I would feel authorized to endorse such legislation after having carefully studied 
the alleged necessity for it and on the condition that I as a member of this house be permitted to debate the principle as well as the regulations for the enforcement of this new form of compulsory service.
However, contrary to what happened in the other provinces, in the constituency of Verdun as in most of the other Quebec constituencies the campaign for an affirmative vote had a counterpart in the strong opposition which was organized and led ever since the plebiscite was announced in the speech from the throne. Radio broadcasts and mass meetings, supported by several of the daily newspapers and by most of the weeklies, appealed for a negative vote on the ground that the question put to the people of Canada, meant conscription, that this was the one and only opportunity the electors had to express an opinion on this veiy important question, and finally, that the Prime Minister left the people entirely free to express their personal and sincere view about it, because he had declared that no vote of confidence was involved in voting on the plebiscite, and he particularly insisted on that in his reply to the telegram which had been sent to him by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) two days before the voting on the plebiscite.
The plebiscite has made known the will of the people of the province of Quebec, but not that of the people in the other provinces, on the very question of conscription for overseas service. It is most unjust and unfair to compare the results of the plebiscite in the province of Quebec with those in the other provinces, because in Quebec there was an organized opposition to the "yes" vote, while in the other eight provinces there was not the slightest organized attempt to show that the vote on the plebiscite was or might be construed as a vote for or against conscription. All the members for the other provinces spoke in the same way to their constituents; and all the newspapers, political clubs, veterans' organizations, trade unions and various social bodies were unanimous in appealing for an affirmative vote on the ground that it did not mean a vote in favour of or against conscription.
The 27th of April was a voting day throughout Canada. It was a real election day. In the eight English-speaking provinces the official candidate of that election was a "yes" vote. Its candidature before the electors was unanimously supported by all organized and public bodies. The candidate did not have any opponent, and so got elected by acclamation.
The victory of April 27th in the other provinces was a victory for the demand of members of parliament and the government for a free

Mobilization Act-Mr. Cote
hand to deal with conscription should the necessity arise, while in Quebec it was a free expression of opinion on the very question of conscription.
If the plebiscite issue had been contested with as much vehemence in the other provinces as in Quebec-and it could have been to judge by the number of negative votes which were cast-the question submitted to the people might have had a different meaning for those electors, and they might have had in mind to vote for or against conscription, as the great majority of the people did in the province of Quebec. In that event the results then might have been very different.
I therefore conclude that if the campaign led in the province of Quebec by the supporters of the negative vote brought the result that we know in most of our constituencies, and if this result is construed as strong opposition in that province to any measure of conscription for overseas service at this time, it does not follow that the results in the other provinces are to be interpreted as a vote on behalf of conscription. I still believe that at this very moment the proportion of our population that would favour this measure even in principle would represent but a minority in the country. I am sure that that is the opinion in my own constituency.
The bill now submitted to the house for second reading is brought down for the purpose of amending the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940. Section 2 of that act is suggested to be amended to read as follows:
The governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things, and make from time to time such orders and regulations, requiring persons to place themselves, their services and their property at the disposal of his majesty in the right of Canada, as may be deemed necessary or expedient for securing the public safety, the defence of Canada, the maintenance of public order, or the efficient prosecution of the war, or for maintaining supplies or services essential to the life of the community.
I now quote the last few lines of section 5 of the act, because they relate to the publication of orders in council:
. . . provided that any of the steps specified in this section may be omitted or deferred if the governor in council considers such omission or deferment necessary in the national interest having regard to the special circumstances.
We all admit, Mr. Speaker, that this is enabling legislation. It empowers the governor in, council to deal from now on, and without any consultation of parliament, with this very question of conscription for overseas service. It will enable the governor in council to decide whether coming events in this war are such that the people of this country will subscribe to a measure of conscription for
overseas service. This amendment gives the governor in council full power to make such decision. The governor in council will also be the only authority to enact compulsory service and to determine the principles and regulations under which this compulsion shall be enforced. Above all, he will not even be bound to make these orders and regulations known to parliament and to the people of the country if he considers that such an attitude on his part is necessary in the national interest under the circumstances.
All hon. members will agree that this bill has been intended by the government and is an attempt to put into effect the affirmative result of the plebiscite. The will of the majority must prevail in this country. I myself will admit that. Knowing the will of the majority of this country, I would be the first to make mine the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1917 and abide by such will. But is it certain that this piece of legislation does not go beyond the will which was expressed by the people on April 27?
Of course the repeal of section 3 of the National Resources Mobilization Act does free the hands of the government. But if this amendment is approved, the mobilization act will have a new bearing which, I submit, will exceed the powers granted by the electors of this country.
Who in this house can say, from the affirmative vote given in the country, it is the will of the people to insert in our statutes at this very moment the principle of conscription without waiting to see whether new circumstances will arise to render it necessary?
Who can say that the affirmative vote was a demand upon members of parliament to yield to the governor in council their privileges as regards the most vital problem that has ever existed in the country in relation to our national unity, and this, before any new circumstances in the nature of those mentioned to the people of Canada during the campaign preceding the plebiscite, have arisen to justify any such surrender to the governor in council?
If the question asked on the plebiscite had been in the following terms, for example, "Do you favour the repeal by parliament of section 3 of the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940?" and if it had been explained to the electors that an affirmative vote would grant to the governor in council full power to put conscription for overseas service into force without any consultation with parliament, at any time that he found the measure to be absolutely necessary, and to enact any regulations to govern the enforcement of that measure of conscription without resort to the advice of or any consultation with members of
Mobilization Act-Mr. Cote

parliament, I wonder what the result would have been in the country. I am sure, knowing my constituency as I do know it, that the affirmative vote on the evening of April 27 would not have given a majority of over 8,600.
In order to get from the country a full expression of its will on this bill, supposed to be the necessary conclusion of the plebiscite, I submit that we should have used the question I have just quoted instead of the one which was indicated on the ballots on April 27. This bill would not then have exceeded the meaning of the plebiscite. As I have just suggested, it would have been a direct sequence of an affirmative vote on the plebiscite.
As a result of the plebiscite we have witnessed a campaign of prejudice and race cries against the province of Quebec, coming from groups of citizens of this country who know the least about Canadians of French descent. They may have come into the province on business purposes, but never have they gone through the experience of a close contact with our French population. Yet these extremists of all sorts have not ceased since April 27 to accuse Quebec of all possible evils in connection with our war effort. I will not insist on the records which Quebec has already set of her will to cooperate in this total war of oura and to contribute to the final victory.
I wish to state that in my opinion this bill before the house has another major aspect. It will help to satisfy and might eventually encourage the feelings which have been developed since April 27 against Quebec by a group of unpatriotic Canadians. This bill in view of its particular implications appears to me to be supported by sentiment rather than by the result and meaning of the plebiscite. Our war effort up to this time, on, both the industrial and military fronts, has been a total and well-balanced war effort, since it would not have been possible to do any better had conscription for overseas service been put into effect a year or two years ago. What is the reason for this change of policy? Our voluntary system is meeting the requirements of the active army in a satisfactory way. Logically, there is no need and no reason for the adoption of this principle at this time. Yet it is proposed to this house to answer the threats of those who want conscription because it is conscription and for no other reason-because in their eyes conscription is the symbol of a total war effort. If we let sentiment overcome common sense and reason in the settlement of such an important problem as that of conscription, we shall render unity impossible in this country. As long as there is not a sincere and deep Canadianism in this dominion, it is not the particular feeling of 
a minority part of a racial group that will serve to unite the country in such a tremendous effort as she is making in this war.
Since the outbreak of war about 25,000 orders in council have been passed by this government to regulate our economic life, war production and military services.
The representatives of the people in parliament have not been consulted about these orders in council, although about three hundred of them were in conflict with some existing statutes. No serious reaction was caused in the country by their enactment, because these regulations were based on logic and not on emotions, and thus the Canadian people have welcomed them in their strong desire to contribute in a total war effort.
I believe, on the other hand, that in my constituency, if not in the whole dominion, my fellow citizens expect that conscription, which has been the vulnerable point of Canadian unity for the past twenty-five years, will remain the exclusive privilege of this parliament to debate and to decide upon whenever circumstances shall arise to render necessary its introduction in this house.
Being a citizen of a free country, I have spoken my mind very freely on this matter of Bill No. 80. In spite of the attitude which I sincerely feel I shall have to take when the bill is put to the vote, let me assure the house that our country is actually making a total war effort and if possible, as circumstances develop, it will be increasing that effort without any objection in my province and in the constituency of Verdun. Moreover, our people in Quebec realize that this is now a Canadian war; that we are fighting for Canada; that we are fighting for our own traditions and creed; that we are fighting for our own salvation. We believe, I for one certainly believe, that the future of Canada being at stake in this war, we cannot ask anything better than that the true Canadian at the head of this country should continue to lead our war effort, with the same success that we have achieved in the past. In spite of the attitude that I shall take on this bill,
I wish to convey to our Prime Minister my sincere admiration and to assure him of my everlasting support notwithstanding that, being a free citizen, I shall again speak my free mind in order to express the opinion of the majority of our population in the constituency of Verdun.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OP SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
It is with some hesitation that I rise to take part in this debate, and were it not for the fact that some of our hon. friends opposite utilized the time at their disposal to make an analysis of the Coopera-

Mobilization Act-Mr. Gillis
tive Commonwealth Federation, its programme and its policy rather than the measure before the house, I might not have decided to take up the time of the house now to discuss this question. But certain things have been said with respect to this group which, in my opinion, require an answer.
The measure before the house is somewhat beclouded. In the discussion to date-and I have listened quite attentively to it-some of our hon. friends have talked exclusively about the plebiscite. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) definitely told the house that this was a conscription bill; he did so without any equivocation. The Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) this afternoon agreed with him to some extent. The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) went to considerable length, with some convincing arguments, to show that the measure was not a conscription measure. Anyone with average intelligence, listening to members of the cabinet, listening to the arguments pro and con, must have had some doubt at times as to what the measure really is. Personally I draw my own conclusions, and regardless of what the programme and policy of this particular group may have been in the past, I am independent and free to exercise my own judgment in this matter or in any other matter that comes before the house.
As one of the members coming from the east coast I wish to point out certain things to the house, instead of discussing simply one phase of the conscription issue as we are doing now. The plebiscite was merely a convenient political trick to offset propaganda coming from political opponents. It was purely and simply a matter of government responsibility. I went out and advocated an affirmative vote, and I did so because I believed in total conscription of everything in Canada necessary to fight the war. An affirmative vote on the plebiscite meant that the road was still open, as far as we were concerned, to push forward in that direction, and I made it absolutely clear to our people that that was our stand then and' would be our stand in the future.
As I see it to-day, what we should be driving home to the Canadian people is the fact that our situation is not merely a matter of conscripting men for military service or of taking over industries to be utilized in an all-out war effort. We should be thinking in Canada to-day in terms of the question whether every man and woman should be seeking some means of learning how to defend themselves. It is not a matter of having 44561-224
to go to the people and requisition them for that service. If they were alive to their own interests and to the seriousness of the international situation, they would be coming, as they should, to the responsible authorities in the country for the formation and organization of means of defence in every section of Canada. Anyone with average intelligence, reading the press to-day, must realize the significance of the statement made by the Prime Minister of Australia on Saturday. He must realize the significance of what is happening on the west coast, where the Japs have a foothold in the Aleutian islands. We have but meagre information on this matter. We do not know where they are. Anyone with average intelligence, I say, must realize the significance of the shelling of Vancouver island, or a section of it, and the shelling of a section of the California coast. This little Jesse James street paper, the Trend, definitely points out-I do not know what its authority is-that within the next ninety days we may expect raids on the east coast. It definitely establishes the fact that German planes a year ago made photographs and a blueprint of everything in that section of the country. That may or may not be true, but as one of the elected representatives of the people I realize-much more I think than they do in central Canada-the seriousness of the situation on both coasts and the necessity for a complete understanding on the part of the people. They will not have that understanding unless they get a lead from their elected representatives. Unfortunately at the present time the complete control of our war effort is in central Canada. While the danger is on both coasts, the control of the machinery necessary to fight the war is in central Canada.
With that background I want to make it clear that as far as the members of this group' are concerned, they are not seizing on the war situation as an opportunity of bringing about in this country a socialist state, as some of our hon. friends opposite accuse us of doing. The programme and policy of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in the light of the war situation is not a political programme; it is a recognition of the fact that if we are to have an all-out war effort to meet those who are waging an all-out war, the complete organization of all the resources of this country is necessary. That is a programme of organization of these resources on the same basis as man-power is expected to be organized under the bill before the house at this time.
On June 11 the leader of our group presented and described in detail a six-point programme

Mobilization Act-Mr. Gillis

of total war effort. Hon. members opposite, instead of discussing the programme on its merits, started calling it names, seeking in that way to frighten the people. They declared that what we" are proposing is state socialism, and that this means regimentation. The habit of referring to our programme as state socialism comes either from ignorance or from deliberate distortion. I want to tell my hon. friends opposite that, after an association of two and a half years with this group, there is no one in this house or outside who is more opposed to state socialism than the members of this group. It ill behooves those on that side of the house to characterize the programme and policy of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation as state socialism, when in reality the government as constituted at the present time is the nearest approach to state socialism of anything we shall ever have in Canada without actually having it.
I am not going to attempt to make an analysis of socialism; there are vague and distorted ideas; but I want to make this clear, particularly to the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) and the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Graham) that what we are fighting against to-day, that totalitarian system, is state socialism. If they succeed in winning this war, the first people that will go to the axeman's block are the members of this group.

Owing to a serious attack of flu I was not able to leave Ottawa during the plebiscite campaign, but I was very much gratified to find that in my absence the constituency of Brandon which I have the honour to represent polled a larger than normal vote and had also the distinction of polling one of the highest percentages of affirmative votes in all the constituencies west of the great lakes, Brandon's percentage being around 92 per cent. I should like here and now to thank a number of the good workers in that constituency who without regard to party or other affiliations got busy and did such a splendid job in the plebiscite campaign. Fifteen thousand or more voters in that constituency
